extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in facial expressions, psychology, anthropology, and social behavior
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and categorize human (and some animal) smiles: anatomical types, evolutionary origins, social functions, cultural variation, and related facial features such as dimples. Useful for readers seeking an overview of how smiles are produced, perceived, and studied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a smile
rubrics_metrics.description: A smile is a facial expression formed primarily by flexing the muscles at the sides of the mouth. Some smiles include a contraction of the muscles at the corner of the eyes, an action known as a Duchenne smile. Among humans, a smile expresses delight, sociability, happiness, joy, or amusement. It is distinct from a similar but usually involuntary expression of anxiety known as a grimace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this anatomical-and-functional definition to distinguish smiles from related facial expressions (e.g., grimaces). Note that smiles may vary cross-culturally in meaning and use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duchenne smile
rubrics_metrics.description: A Duchenne smile engages the muscles around the mouth and eyes. It involves contraction of both the zygomatic major muscle (which raises the corners of the mouth) and the orbicularis oculi muscle (which raises the cheeks and forms crow's feet around the eyes). The Duchenne smile has been described as 'smizing', as in 'smiling with the eyes'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers associate Duchenne smiles uniquely with positive emotion. Anatomical identification (zygomatic major + orbicularis oculi) is the criterion for classifying a smile as Duchenne. Recent tools (e.g., Dynasmile) perform video-based Duchenne analysis for orthodontics/behavioral study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Duchenne smile
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-Duchenne smile involves only the zygomatic major muscle (raising the lip corners) and does not engage the orbicularis oculi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically considered a generic index of joy, more recent research differentiates it from Duchenne smiles; non-Duchenne smiles are less uniquely linked to genuine positive emotion and can function as social/posed smiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pan Am ('Botox') smile / fake smile
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Pan Am smile', also known as the 'Botox smile', is a fake smile in which only the zygomatic major muscle is voluntarily contracted to show politeness. It is named after Pan American World Airways flight attendants who displayed a perfunctory smile to passengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize Pan Am smiles as social/posed signals rather than necessarily genuine positive affect. Chronic Botox around the eyes can prevent orbicularis oculi contraction and thus block Duchenne smiles, producing a persistent non-Duchenne appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social effects of smiling
rubrics_metrics.description: Smiling seems to have a favorable influence upon others and makes one likable and more approachable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In social sequences, smiling can act as a pre-laughing device (paving the way to laughter) or as a response to laughter. Use awareness of these functions when interpreting social interactions—smiles may initiate, accompany, or follow other affiliative behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smiling as reinforcement and manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of smiling on others is not necessarily benign. It may take the form of positive reinforcement, possibly for an underhand manipulative and abusive purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to contexts where smiling is used instrumentally to influence or manipulate; the presence of a smile does not guarantee goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural differences in smiling
rubrics_metrics.description: Smiling frequency, acceptability, and interpretation vary by culture. Researchers found smiles more common in the U.S. and France than in China or Japan (in photos and observed life). In some cultures smiling is perceived as negative, unwelcoming, a sign of shallowness or dishonesty, or used to indicate embarrassment or emotional pain. In parts of the former Soviet Union, smiling at strangers may be unusual or suspicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating smiles cross-culturally, consider local norms: frequency in photos, who smiles with whom (strangers vs close friends), and culturally-specific interpretations (e.g., intelligence/honesty judgments). Social-level factors (e.g., corruption) can modulate how smiles are perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary background of the smile
rubrics_metrics.description: The smile can be traced to a 'fear grin' in primates, used to portray harmlessness or signal submission; it may have evolved differently among species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evolutionary accounts to interpret homologous facial displays in nonhuman primates and to explain some social functions (submission, appeasement) of human smiling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimples as a facial feature related to smiling
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheek dimples are formed secondary to a bifid zygomaticus major muscle whose fascial strands insert into the dermis and cause a dermal tethering effect. Dimples are genetically inherited and are a dominant trait. Bilateral dimples are most common; single (unilateral) dimples are rarer. Face shape affects dimple appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing or classifying smiles, note presence/absence and type of dimples (bilateral vs single) as a morphological characteristic; literature also addresses surgical creation and prevalence studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smiling and teeth-baring in other animals
rubrics_metrics.description: In other animals, baring of teeth is often a threat or warning display (a snarl) or a sign of submission; for chimpanzees it can signal fear. Some species (e.g., Barbary macaques) display an open-mouth play face that is likely similar in roots and purpose to the human smile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the same facial configuration carries the same meaning across species—interpret animal 'smiles' in ethological context; some displays may be homologous (play/affiliative) while others are antagonistic.
